Q: Microsoft Graph API: Intune Win32 App Upload - commitFileFailed Error After Successful API Calls A:

our setup matches a well-known failure mode: you mentioned Upload Method: Single PUT (files < 4MB per Microsoft guidance), and that's almost certainly the cause. Here's why it breaks.

The SAS URI Azure gives you is a Block Blob endpoint, not a simple object store. When you do a single-part PUT directly to it, Azure Storage accepts the data (HTTP 200), but it never commits a block list. Intune's post-commit step then asks Azure to verify the uploaded content against a block list that doesn't exist, and that's what produces commitFileFailed. The HTTP success from step 5 is misleading — the failure is in Intune's backend validation, not in the upload itself.

The fix is to use the Block Blob multi-part protocol even for small files:

import base64, requests

def chunked_upload(sas_uri: str, file_path: str, chunk_mb: int = 6) -> None:
    chunk_size = chunk_mb * 1024 * 1024
    block_ids = []
    with open(file_path, "rb") as f:
        index = 0
        while True:
            chunk = f.read(chunk_size)
            if not chunk:
                break
            block_id = base64.b64encode(f"block-{index:06d}".encode()).decode()
            block_ids.append(block_id)
            requests.put(
                f"{sas_uri}&comp=block&blockid={block_id}",
                data=chunk,
                headers={"x-ms-blob-type": "BlockBlob"},
            ).raise_for_status()
            index += 1
    # This commit step is what was missing
    xml = '<?xml version="1.0"?><BlockList>'
    xml += "".join(f"<Latest>{b}</Latest>" for b in block_ids)
    xml += "</BlockList>"
    requests.put(
        f"{sas_uri}&comp=blocklist",
        data=xml,
        headers={"Content-Type": "application/xml"},
    ).raise_for_status()

A secondary thing to check: your fileEncryptionInfo payload includes "@odata.type": "microsoft.graph.fileEncryptionInfo". Remove it. That annotation is not expected here and can cause Intune's schema validation to silently fail even when all the field values are correct. The seven fields that work are encryptionKey, macKey, initializationVector, mac, profileIdentifier, fileDigest, and fileDigestAlgorithm — nothing else in that object.

If you fix the upload protocol and still see the error, check that the SAS URI hasn't expired (it's valid for roughly an hour). Renew it with POST /contentVersions/{id}/files/{fileId}/renewUpload if you're retrying after a delay.

For a full end-to-end walkthrough of all six steps including how to extract the encryption fields from Detection.xml inside the .intunewin ZIP, I wrote this up in PowerShell here: https://jocha.se/blog/tech/automating-intune-win32-app-packaging-with-github-actions (disclosure: my blog, but the API flow is the same in any language).

Q: Apache Spark 3.3.0 breaks on Java 17 with "cannot access class sun.nio.ch.DirectBuffer" A:

Following step helped me to unblock the issue.

If you are running the application from IDE (intelliJ IDEA) follow the below instructions.

Add the JVM option "--add-exports java.base/sun.nio.ch=ALL-UNNAMED"

Q: What's the difference between DETACHED_PROCESS and CREATE_NO_WINDOW process creation flags for CreateProcess function? A:

I have not tested what Hans Passant said about AttachConsole(ATTACH_PARENT_PROCESS). However, I have found another difference based on testing.

Let's define a process tree to better explain what I mean:

A
|
+-- B
    |
    +-- C

With DETACH_PROCESS, only the started process (B) has no console — by default. If the started process starts console child processes (C), then each of those child process will be started in a new console. Furthermore, the started process B (or its children C) can still create a console by calling AllocConsole.

CREATE_NO_WINDOW is a "nuclear option" that's stronger than DETACH_PROCESS. Even the started process' children (C) don't get a console, not even if they call AllocConsole. Furthermore, Ctrl-C'ing the topmost process (A) won't terminate B and C, so it seems that CREATE_NO_WINDOW also includes an effect similar to starting a new process group.

Q: Does "nonisolated(sending) by Default" setting conflict with "Default actor isolation" setting in Xcode 26? A:

There are two very separate issues at play:

  1. You have identified the historic asymmetry with regard to nonisolated functions, namely where synchronous ones ran on the current thread but asynchronous ones introduced a context hop. “Approachable concurrency” arguably rectifies this, bringing these two into line, where all nonisolated functions simply avoid unnecessary context hops, whether synchronous or asynchronous.

    And, in those cases where one actually want the context hop in the async functions, use @concurrent.

    This behavior is dictated by the “nonisolated(nonsending) by default” build setting. If “Yes”, it follows the behavior I outline above. If “No”, we have the legacy behavior.

  2. The above notwithstanding, “approachable concurrency” acknowledges a separate, but deep truth: Writing thread-safe code can be complicated, but calling asynchronous API doesn’t need to be. They realized that the bulk of applications operate perfectly well if the whole thing is isolated to the main actor (and merely await asynchronous API). And the beauty of defaulting everything to the main actor is that vast swaths of thread-safety concerns (Sendable types, region-based isolation, etc.) just evaporate.

    So “approachable concurrency” basically steers us towards “keep it simple and default to the main actor where reasonable.” They suggest only introducing thread-safety complexities when it is really needed (notably, where you might be doing something slow and synchronous). And even then, in those rare cases where we need to introduce multithreading (e.g., actors, @concurrent functions, etc.), we are no worse off than we were before Swift 6.2.

    But, now we can simply sidestep this complexity when it is not needed.

    This behavior is dictated by the “Default actor” build setting. If “MainActor”, we get this new (easier) behavior. If “nonisolated”, we get the legacy behavior.

Now, both of these build settings reference “nonisolated”, but there is no inherent conflict between them; they are simply solving two very different problems. But, for new apps, at least, the default build settings are probably well advised:

Build setting Default value in new apps Description
“nonisolated(nonsending) by default” “Yes” Consistency of nonisolated functions, whether synchronous or asynchronous
“Default actor” “MainActor” Eliminate many unnecessary multithreaded considerations

Q: bash: extracting last two dirs for a pathname A:

11 years later: saving a few characters on Chris F.A. Johnson's answer. Needs bash 4+ for negative subscripts.

$ DIRNAME=a/b/c/d/e
$ IFS=/ dirs=($DIRNAME)
$ echo ${dirs[-2]}/${dirs[-1]}
d/e
